idiom_name: Proc#>> and Proc#<< (with Method#to_proc) over Enumerable
implementation_notes: Ruby core implements the pattern's essence: since 2.6 `Proc#>>` and `Proc#<<` compose a proc with another proc, a method or any object responding to `call`, returning a new callable - so a pipeline is a value you can pass around, and `Enumerable#map/#select/#reduce` covers the collection side. Nothing here is replaced by a class hierarchy: the DSL is built from lambdas plus composition. The classic structure is still warranted when the steps need names, configuration or introspection (a small builder object, or a gem such as dry-monads for railway-style results).
pitfalls: Proc versus lambda semantics survive composition: a non-lambda proc returns from the enclosing method and pads missing arguments, so compose lambdas when strict behaviour is expected.
Composition preserves the left operand's flavour only: a chain that starts from a proc stays a proc (lenient arity), even when the right operand is a lambda.
Closures capture variables by reference, and composition does not freeze them - a composed proc observes later mutations of the captured local.

variants.name: Enumerator::Lazy chains
variants.implementation_notes: `Enumerable#lazy` turns the collection combinators into a lazy chain: `map`, `select`, `reject`, `flat_map` and `take_while` on a `Enumerator::Lazy` build another lazy enumerator instead of evaluating, and nothing runs until a terminal method (`first`, `to_a`/`force`) is called, so infinite sequences compose. This is the pattern realized as a lazy transformation pipeline rather than as function composition; choose it when the input is large or unbounded, and remember the documented tradeoff that each lazy step adds generator overhead for small collections.
variants.code_sketch:
naturals = (1..Float::INFINITY).lazy
squares = naturals.map { |n| n * n }
even = squares.select(&:even?)
puts even.first(3).inspect      # [4, 16, 36]
puts even.take(3).force.inspect # materialise on demand
pitfalls: A lazy chain needs a terminating operation: passing an unbounded chain to a method that enumerates everything never returns.
`Enumerator::Lazy` only redefines part of `Enumerable`: any other method forces full enumeration and silently materialises the chain.
Generator overhead: for small collections the eager version is faster, which the documentation explicitly warns about.
